task.title: Simpson's Paradox: University Admissions
task.prompt:
A university has two departments: Engineering and Arts.

Engineering: admitted 30/100 men (30%) and 20/50 women (40%)
Arts: admitted 300/400 men (75%) and 350/400 women (87.5%)

Overall: admitted 330/500 men (66%) and 370/450 women (82.2%)

A journalist writes: "The university discriminates against men — only 66% of male
applicants were admitted versus 82.2% of female applicants."

Is this claim valid? Explain why or why not with precise reasoning.
task.context:
This task tests whether the solver can identify Simpson's paradox — where a trend that
appears in aggregated data reverses when the data is separated into subgroups.
task.reference_solution:
The claim is misleading. Within each department, men are admitted at a LOWER rate than women:
- Engineering: men 30%, women 40% — women favored
- Arts: men 75%, women 87.5% — women favored
The aggregate reversal happens because men disproportionately applied to the more selective
department (Engineering). This is Simpson's paradox. The per-department data shows no
discrimination against men.

parsed.final_answer: The journalist's claim is misleading. This is Simpson's Paradox. While the aggregate data shows men admitted at 66% vs women at 82.2%, within each department women actually have higher admission rates. Engineering: men 30%, women 40%. Arts: men 75%, women 87.5%. The reversal occurs because men disproportionately applied to Engineering, which has much lower admission rates overall.
assumptions: The admission data as presented is accurate and complete
Department assignment is based on applicant choice, not university assignment
steps: First, I verify the department-level data: Engineering admits 30% of men and 40% of women.
In Arts, men are admitted at 75% and women at 87.5% — women have higher rates in both departments.
The aggregate reversal happens because 80% of men (400/500) applied to the less selective Arts department, while a larger share of men applied to the more selective Engineering department.
This is Simpson's Paradox: the trend that appears in aggregated data reverses when disaggregated by department.

The causal mechanism is that department choice acts as a confounding variable — men apply more to the selective department, which drives down their aggregate rate despite being admitted at lower rates in each department.
alternative_hypotheses: The university intentionally discriminates against men — rejected because department-level data shows women are favored in both departments, and the aggregate pattern is fully explained by application composition
uncertainties: Whether applicant qualifications differ between men and women within each department
Whether there are additional departments not shown in this data
self_check: Verified arithmetic: 30/100=30%, 20/50=40% in Engineering; 300/400=75%, 350/400=87.5% in Arts. Overall: 330/500=66% men, 370/450=82.2% women. All numbers check out.
Could I be falling for a different statistical trap? No — the reversal pattern is clear and the confounding variable (department choice) fully explains the aggregate reversal.

Simpson's Paradox explains the aggregate reversal
Department choice is the confounding variable
